translations.text: I have heard that far from here, in the eastern regions, lies the noblest of lands, famous among men.
That region of the earth is not within reach of many rulers of peoples across the world. Through the Creator's might it is set apart from those who do evil.
That plain is all beautiful, gladdened with joys, with the fairest fragrances of the earth.
Peerless is that island, noble the maker, proud and abundant in power, who established that land.
There the door of the heavenly kingdom is often open toward the blessed, and the joy of its songs is revealed.
That is a delightful plain, with green woods, spacious under the skies. Neither rain nor snow, nor the breath of frost, nor the blast of fire, nor the fall of hail, nor the descent of rime,
nor the heat of the sun, nor perpetual cold, nor warm weather, nor winter shower can do any harm there, but the plain remains blessed and unharmed. That noble land is blooming with flowers.

No hills or steep mountains stand there, nor do stone cliffs tower high, as here with us; there are no valleys or dales or mountain caves, no mounds or ridges, nor does anything rough ever lie there, but the noble field flourishes under the clouds, blooming with delights.

That bright land is twelve fathoms higher by measure of the earth, as wise prophets [?] make known to us in writings through their wisdom, than any of the hills that here tower brightly and high among us under the stars of heaven.
Calm is that plain of victory; the sunny grove gleams, the delightful forest. The fruits, the bright produce, do not fall, but the trees stand ever green, as God commanded them.
In winter and in summer alike the wood is hung with fruit; the leaves under the sky never decay, nor will flame ever harm them, until a change comes upon the world.

Long ago, when the might of the waters, the sea-flood, covered all of middle-earth, the whole circuit of the earth, that noble plain, wholly unharmed, stood preserved against the onrush of the fierce waves, blessed and unblemished, through the grace of God;
it will remain thus blooming until the coming of the fire, the Lord's judgment, when the halls of death, the dark chambers of men, will be opened.

In that land there is no hostile enemy, no weeping or vengeance, no sign of woe, neither old age nor misery nor narrow death, nor loss of life, nor the coming of harm, nor sin nor strife nor painful suffering,

…neither the struggle of poverty nor the lack of wealth, nor sorrow, nor sleep, nor grievous sickness, nor winter's storm, nor change of weather, fierce under the heavens, nor the hard frost with its cold icicles strikes anyone there.
there neither hail nor frost falls to the earth, nor windy cloud, nor does water fall there, driven by the wind, but there streams, wondrously beautiful, spring up as wells in fair surging floods.
Delightful waters moisten the earth from the midst of the wood; each month they break out, sea-cold, from the turf of the soil and flow through the whole grove, at times mightily.
It is the Prince's command that twelve times the joy of the flowing waters should play across that glorious land.
The groves are hung with fruits, beautiful produce; there the ornaments of the forest, holy under the heavens, never diminish.

No faded blossoms fall to the ground there, and the beauty of the forest trees does not fall away. Instead, the branches on the trees there are always wondrously laden, and the fruit is renewed. At all times they stand green on the grassy plain, joyfully adorned by the might of the Holy One, the brightest of groves.

The forest's color is never impaired, where the holy fragrance dwells throughout the land of delight; that will never be changed, until the Wise One who created it in the beginning brings his ancient work to an end.
That wood is guarded by a wondrously fair bird, strong of feather, which is called the phoenix.
There the solitary one keeps its dwelling and lives its brave life; never will death harm it on that pleasant plain as long as the world stands.

It must watch the course of the sun and come toward God's candle, the shining gem, eagerly watching for the time when the noblest of stars rises over the wave-sea, shining from the east, the Father's ancient work gleaming with adornment, the bright sign of God.
The stars are hidden, gone under the waves into the western regions, concealed at dawn, and the dark night departs in gloom;

Then the bird, strong in its flight and proud in its feathers, looks eagerly out over the ocean beneath the sky and over the sea, waiting for the light of heaven to come gliding up from the east over the wide sea.
So the noble bird, steadfast in its beauty, stays by the welling streams at the spring. There the glorious one bathes himself twelve times in the brook before the coming of the beacon,
the candle of the sky. Each time, at every bath, he tastes the sea-cold water of the pleasant springs.

Then, after his play in the water, the high-spirited bird lifts himself onto a tall tree. From there he can most easily watch the eastern ways for the journey of heaven's taper, when it gleams brightly over the tossing sea, the radiance of light.
The lands are adorned and the world made beautiful once the gem of glory, the most glorious of stars, shines over the ocean's course and over the ground throughout the world.
As soon as the sun rises high above the salt streams, the grey bird leaves the tree in the grove, bright, and goes swift-feathered in flight through the air. He makes melody and sings toward the sky.
Then the bird's bearing is very fair, his heart inspired and exultant with joy;
he varies his song skilfully in a bright voice, more wondrously than any son of man has ever heard under the heavens since the High King, the maker of glory, established the world, heaven and earth.
The sound of that song is sweeter and more beautiful than all the arts of song, and more delightful than any melody.

Nothing can equal that sound: not trumpets or horns, not the sound of the harp, not the voice of any man on earth, not the organ with its harmonious song, not the swan's feathers, nor any of the joys that the Lord created for the delight of men in this sorrowful world.
So he sings and makes melody, gladdened with happiness, until the sun has sunk into the southern sky.
Then he falls silent and listens. He lifts his head, bold and wise in thought, and three times shakes his flight-swift feathers; the bird is silent.
Always he marks the hours twelve times, by day and by night.

So it is ordained for the dweller in the grove that he may enjoy the plain there with delight and make use of its wealth, life and pleasures, and the adornments of the land, until he, guardian of the woodland grove, has lived a thousand winters of this life.

Then the grey-feathered one is weighed down, old and full of years. The joy of birds flies away from the green earth, the blossoming land, and seeks a wide realm of the world where no men inhabit land or homeland.

There, very mighty, he receives lordship over the race of birds and is honoured among that people, and for a time he guards the wilderness with them. Then, strong in flight but burdened with winters, he departs westward, flying swift-feathered.
Birds throng around the noble one. Each of them wishes to be a thane and servant to the glorious lord, until they reach the land of the Syrians in the greatest of companies.
There the pure one quickly slips away from them, so that he dwells in the shade, in a woodland grove, a deserted place, concealed and hidden from most men.
There he inhabits and guards a tall tree in the forest, firmly rooted under the roof of heaven. Men on earth call it Phoenix, after the bird's name.
The King mighty in glory, the Lord of mankind, has granted that tree, as I have heard, that of all the trees growing up on the earth it alone blossoms most brightly;
nothing bitter can harm it, but it remains shielded forever and unharmed for as long as the world stands.
When the wind is still, the weather is fair, and heaven's holy gem shines clear, the clouds are scattered and the mighty waters stand still,
every storm is calmed under the sky, and the warm candle of the weather gleams from the south and gives light to the peoples, then he begins to build in the branches and to prepare a nest.
He has great need to turn his old age quickly back to life, through the surging of his mind, and to receive young life.
Then from far and near he collects and gathers the sweetest, most delightful herbs and fruits of the forest into that dwelling place, every noble fragrance
of delightful herbs, the sweetest under the sky, which the King of glory, Father of every beginning, created over the earth as a noble gift for the race of men.
There he himself carries bright treasures into that tree; there the wild bird in the wilderness builds a house high in the lofty tree, beautiful and delightful,
…and dwells there itself in the upper chamber. In the shade of the leaves it surrounds its body and feathers on every side with holy fragrances and the noblest blossoms of the earth.

It sits, eager for the journey. Then heaven's gem, the sun, at its hottest in summertime, shines over the shadows, carries out its appointed course, and looks out over the world. Then the bird's house becomes heated by the bright sky.
The herbs grow warm, and the pleasant hall steams with sweet scents. Then, in the heat, the bird burns along with its nest in the grip of the fire.
The pyre is kindled. Then the fire covers the house of the sorely wounded one and rushes fiercely on. The yellow flame consumes it, and the phoenix burns, old and wise with the years of long ago.
Then the fire consumes the transient body. Life departs, the life-hoard of the doomed one, when the flame of the pyre burns flesh and bone.
Yet after a time life comes back to it, renewed, once the ashes, after the violence of the fire, begin to lock together again, clustered into a ball.
Then the brightest of nests, the dwelling of the battle-brave one, is wholly consumed by fire. The body grows cold, the bone-vessel is broken, and the burning dies down.
Then the likeness of an apple is found again in the ash of the pyre. From it grows a worm, wondrously fair, as if it had come out of an egg, bright from the shell.
Then it grows in the shade, so that at first it is like an eagle's chick, a fair young bird;
then further [?] it grows in joy, until in form it is like an old eagle, and after that it is adorned with feathers, as it was at the beginning, brightly blossoming.

Then the flesh becomes entirely renewed, born again, separated from sins. It is somewhat as when people bring home the fruits of the earth for sustenance at harvest, delightful food, before winter comes,

at the time of reaping, so that a shower of rain does not ruin them under the clouds. There they find support and the joy of feasting when frost and snow cover the earth with overwhelming power in winter garments.
From those fruits the wealth of men will spring again through the nature of the grain, which is first sown as clean seed.
Then the gleam of the sun in spring, the sign of life, awakens the world's treasure, so that the fruits, the ornaments of the earth, are born again through their own nature.
In the same way the bird, old after many years, becomes young and renewed, clothed in flesh.

He takes no food, no meat on the earth, except that he tastes a portion of honeydew, which often falls at midnight. With this the brave one nourishes his life until he seeks out again his ancient seat, his own land.
Then the bird, proud in his feathers, has grown up among the herbs. His life is new, young, full of gifts. Then, nimble of limb, he gathers up from the dust his body,
which the flame had earlier consumed. He gathers the remnants of the burning, skilfully collects the decayed bones after the violence of the pyre, and then he brings the bones and ashes
…the remains of the pyre, together again. Then it covers the spoil of slaughter with herbs, beautifully adorned. Then it is eager to seek its own homeland again.
Then he clasps the remains of the fire with his feet, grips them in his claws, and joyfully seeks again his homeland, the sun-bright dwellings, the blessed native land.
All is renewed, life and coat of feathers, as he was at the beginning, when God, the victorious, first set him in that noble plain.

There it brings its own bones, which the surge of fire had earlier engulfed in the blaze on the pyre-place [?], together with the ashes. Then the one strong in battle buries everything together, bones and ashes, on that island.
The sign of the sun is renewed for him when the light of heaven, gladdest of gems, the joy of the noble stars, shines up from the east over the ocean.
The bird is fair in colour at the front, adorned with shimmering hues about the front of the breast.
His head is green at the back, wondrously variegated, mingled with purple.
His tail is beautifully divided: part brown, part crimson, part skilfully set with shining spots.
The feathers are white at the back, and the neck is green below and above. The beak shines like glass or a gem, and the jaws are bright inside and out.
The eye is fierce, and in its colour most like a stone, a bright gem, when it is set in a vessel of gold by the skill of smiths.
Around the neck, like the ring of the sun, is the brightest of rings, woven of feathers.
The belly underneath is splendid, wondrously fair, bright and shining. Above, over the bird's back, the shield is joined with ornaments.
Its legs are covered with scales, and its feet are yellow. In its colouring the bird is unique in every way, most like a peacock, grown up in joys, as the writings say.

He is not sluggish or slothful, nor heavy and slow like some birds that flap lazily through the air on their feathers. He is quick and swift and very light, beautiful and delightful, marked with glory.
Eternal is the Prince who grants him that bliss!
Then he departs from this native soil to seek the plains, his old homeland.
As the bird flies, he shows himself to peoples, to many men throughout the world. Then they gather in troops from south and north, from east and west,

and travel from far and near in hosts of people to where they may see the Creator's grace shown fairly in the bird, since at the beginning the true King of victories gave him a more wondrous nature and fairer adornments than the rest of the race of birds.

Then men across the earth marvel at his beauty and his form. They make it known in writings and carve with their hands on marble stone when the day and the hour showed the people the adornments of the swift flier.

Then the race of birds throngs in flocks from every side. They swoop down along wide ways, praise him with song, and glorify the proud one with mighty voices. So they encircle the holy one in a ring as they fly through the air. The phoenix is in the middle, surrounded by the throngs.

The peoples gaze and marvel in wonder at how the willing company honours the wild one, crowd after crowd. They show their skills and glorify the beloved lord of the people as their king, and with joy they lead the noble one to his land,
until the solitary one flies off, swift of feather, so that the company of rejoicers cannot follow him, when the joy of hosts leaves the soil of this earth to seek his homeland.
So after the time of death the blessed one visits his old home again, the fair land. Sad at heart, the birds turn away from the battle-bold one and go back to their own land.
Then the prince is young in his dwelling. God alone, the almighty King, knows what his nature is, whether female or male;
no one of the race of men knows it, only the Lord alone, how wondrous the ways are, the fair ancient decree, concerning the bird's birth.
There the blessed one may enjoy his homeland and the welling streams in the forest groves, and dwell on the plain until a thousand winters have run their course.
Then the end of life comes to him. The pyre covers him with kindled fire. Yet he comes back to life afterwards, wondrously awakened.

Therefore it does not dread drooping death or the painful agony of dying, since it always knows that after the violence of the fire it will have life renewed, life after its fall. Then, in the form of a young bird, it is vigorously revived again from the ash and grows young again under the shelter of the sky.
It is itself both son and dear father, and also always the heir of its own old remains.
The mighty Creator of mankind granted it that it should become again, so wondrously, the same thing it was before, clothed in feathers, even though fire takes it.

In the same way each of the blessed chooses eternal life for himself through dark death, after grievous pain, so that after his days of old he may enjoy the Lord's gifts in everlasting joys, and afterwards dwell forever in glory as a reward for his works.

The nature of this bird is in many ways a sign to the cities of Christ's chosen servants: how through the Father's help they hold on to bright joy under the heavens in this perilous time, and win for themselves exalted glory in the heavenly homeland.
We have heard that the Almighty made man and woman through the abundance of his wonders, and then set them in the best of the regions of the earth,
The children of men call it Paradise. There they lacked no bliss of any kind, as long as they were willing to keep the word of the Eternal One, the utterance of the Holy One, in that new joy.
There enmity harmed them, the envy of the old fiend, who offered them food, the fruit of the tree, so that both of them unwisely ate the apple against God's will and tasted what was forbidden.
There misery turned bitter for them after the eating, and for their offspring likewise: a painful feast for sons and daughters.

Their teeth [?] were grievously paid back for the sin. They had God's anger and bitter, baleful sorrow. Afterwards their children paid dearly for this, because they had eaten that food against the word of the Eternal One.

Therefore, sad at heart, they had to give up the joy of their homeland because of the serpent's malice, when with a treacherous spirit it cruelly deceived our first parents in days of old. So they went far from there to seek a dwelling in this valley of death, a more sorrowful place to live.

The better life was hidden from them in darkness, and the holy plain was firmly shut through the fiend's cunning for a multitude of winters, until the King of glory, the joy of mankind, comforter of the weak and the only hope, opened it again for the holy ones through his coming here.
This bird's journey is most like this, as the learned tell us in words and as writings make known: when, old in years, he gives up land and homeland and has grown aged.
It departs weary at heart, burdened by winters, to where it finds the high shelter of a wood. There, out of twigs and the noblest herbs, it builds a new dwelling, a nest in the grove.

He has great need that he, aged in life, may receive life again after death through the blast of flame, may be young again, and may seek his old home, the sun-bright dwellings, after the bath of fire.

So the forebears, our ancestors, abandoned the beautiful plain and the seat of glory, lovely, behind them, and made a long journey into the hands of harmful ones, where enemies, wretched monsters, often injured them.
Yet there were many who obeyed the Creator well under the heavens with holy practices and glorious deeds, so that the Lord, the high King of the heavens, became gracious to them in mind.
That is the high tree in which the holy now keep their dwelling, where none of the ancient enemies can harm them at all with poison, with the token of treachery, in this perilous time.
There the Lord's champion builds himself a nest against every enmity with glorious deeds, when he gives alms to the poor and to those without means, and calls on the Lord, the Father, for help,
hastens onward. He quenches the sins of this passing life, the dark evil deeds. He keeps the Lord's law firm in his heart, seeks out prayer with pure thoughts, and nobly bends his knee to the earth,

Each one flees every evil and grim sin for fear of God, and glad of heart desires to accomplish the greatest of good deeds. For him the Lord is a shield on every journey: the Ruler of victories, the gracious giver to the hosts.
These are the herbs, the blossoms of fruits, which the wild bird gathers far and wide under the sky to his dwelling-place, where he builds a nest wondrously firm against every hostility.
So now in those dwellings the Creator's champions do his will with mind and might and strive for glorious deeds; for this the eternal Almighty will repay them with a blessed reward.
From those herbs a dwelling is built for them in the city of glory, as a reward for their works, because they kept the holy teaching burning in their hearts,
With fervent spirit they love the Lord day and night, and with bright faith they choose the Beloved above worldly wealth. They take no joy or hope in living long in this passing life.
Thus the blessed man courageously earns eternal joy, a home in the heavens with the high King, until the end of his number of days comes, when death, the slaughter-greedy warrior,

armed with weapons, takes the life of each one, and swiftly sends the transient bodies, deprived of their souls, into the embrace of the earth, where they remain a long time covered by soil until the coming of the fire.
Then many of the race of men will be led to the assembly; the Father of angels, the true King of victories, the Lord of hosts, will hold a synod to judge with justice.
Then all men on earth will rise again, as the mighty King, the Prince of angels, the Saviour of souls, commands with the trumpet's voice over the wide earth.
Dark death will be ended for the blessed by the Lord's might. The noble ones will go forth and throng in troops, when this sin-working world burns in shame, kindled as a pyre.

Each one will become afraid in spirit when fire breaks up the transient wealth of the land, when flame consumes all the treasure of the earth, greedily seizes the embossed gold, and ravenously swallows the ornaments of the land.

Then, in that open time, the fair and joyful token of this bird will come to light for men, when the Power raises all up from the graves, gathers bones, limbs and body together, and the spirit of life, before Christ's knee.
The King, the beautiful gem of glory, will shine gloriously upon the holy from his high throne. It will be well for the one who may please God in that sorrowful time.
There the bodies, clean of sins, will go glad of heart, and the spirits will return into their bone-vessels, when the burning rises high to heaven.
Hot for many will be the terrible fire, when each one, righteous and sinful, soul with body, comes from the graves of earth to seek the Creator's judgment, struck with terror.
The fire will be set in motion and will burn up vice. There the blessed, after their time of exile, will be clothed in their works, their own deeds.

that these noble things are the pleasant herbs with which the wild bird surrounds his own nest on the outside, so that it suddenly burns with fire and is scorched under the sun, and he himself with it, and then after the flame he receives life again, anew.

So it is with each one of the race of men, clothed in flesh: he becomes unique and young again, if here by his own will he works so that the mighty King of glory will be merciful to him at that assembly.

Then holy spirits will sing out, righteous souls, pure and chosen. They will raise a song and praise the King's majesty, voice after voice, and they will rise to glory, beautifully fragrant with their good deeds as if with herbs.
Then the spirits of men will be refined, brightly cleansed through the burning of fire.
Let no one of the human race think that I put together a song out of lying words, or write by the craft of poetry. Hear the prophecy of Job's songs.
Inspired in his breast by the glory of the Spirit, he spoke boldly, honoured with glory; he said these words:
"I do not scorn, in the thoughts of my heart, to choose a deathbed in my nest, a man weary in body, and to depart from there, humbled, on a long journey, covered in clay, sad about my former deeds,

into the embrace of the earth. And then, after death, through the Lord's grace, like the bird phoenix, I may have renewed life after the resurrection, and joys with the Lord, where the dear company praises the Beloved One.
I can never, for all time, live to see the end of that life, of light and joys.
Though my body must rot in the earth-house, to the pleasure of worms, yet the God of hosts will release my soul after the time of death and raise it up into glory.
This hope will never break in my breast, since I hold firmly to lasting joy in the Prince of angels."

So in ancient days the wise man, prudent of mind, God's messenger, sang of his resurrection into eternal life, so that we might more eagerly understand the glorious sign that the bright bird shows through its burning.
After the burning, the bird gathers up all that is left of the bones, the ashes and cinders. Then it carries them in its feet to the Lord's courts, toward the sun.
There they will dwell from then on for many winters, renewed in growth, entirely young again, where no one in that nation can threaten them with hostility.

So now after death, through the Lord's might, souls will travel together with the body, beautifully adorned, very like the bird, into blessed riches with noble fragrances, where the true sun shines in beauty over the hosts in the city of glory.
when Christ the Saviour shines high over the roofs on the souls of the righteous.
Shining birds follow him, made bright and new again, exulting in bliss, into that glad home: chosen spirits, eternal forever.
There the hostile, shameless fiend cannot harm them with evil deceit. Instead they will live there for ever, clothed in light, like the bird phoenix, in the Lord's protection, beautiful in glory.
Each one's work will shine brightly in that joyful home before the face of the eternal Lord, ever in peace, like the sun.
There a bright crown, wondrously woven with precious stones, rises above the head of each of the blessed. Their heads shine, covered with majesty.

The Prince's royal gold wonderfully adorns each of the righteous with light in life, where the long joy, eternal and ever young, never fades. Instead they dwell in beauty, surrounded by glory and fair adornments, with the Father of angels.
In those dwellings there is nothing at all to grieve them: no strife, no want, no days of toil, no burning hunger, no hard thirst, no misery, no old age.
The noble King gives them every good thing. There the host of spirits praises the Saviour and proclaims the might of the King of heaven; they sing praise to the Creator.
The peaceful host resounds clearly with the greatest of sounds around God's holy high throne. The blessed, together with the angels, joyfully bless the best of lords with one voice, saying:
"Peace be to you, true God, and the power of wisdom, and thanks be to you, who sit in majesty, for new gifts, for every good thing.

Great, immeasurable in the strength of your might, high and holy! The heavens are beautifully filled, Father almighty, glory of all glories, with your glory, above among the angels and on earth as well.
Protect us, Creator of all beginnings! You are the Father almighty in the highest, ruler of the heavens."

So speak those who do right, cleansed of sin, in that glorious city. The company of the righteous proclaim his royal majesty and sing the Emperor's praise in the sky. To him alone belongs eternal honour, forever without end.

His beginning never was, nor any origin of his blessedness. Though he was born here on earth in the form of a child into this world, the abundance of his powers still remained high above the heavens, holy, his glory unbroken.
Though he had to suffer the agony of death on the tree of the cross, a cruel torment, on the third day after his body fell he received life again through the Father's help.
So the phoenix, young in its dwellings, signifies the might of God's Son, when it wakes again from the ashes into the life of life, flourishing in its limbs.

Just as the Saviour brought us help, life without end, through the parting from his body, so the bird fills its two wings with sweet and delightful herbs, the fair fruits of the earth, when it is eager to set out.
These are the words, as the writings tell us, the voice of the holy ones, whose mind is turned to the heavens, to the merciful God,
a mind hastening into the joy of joys, where, as a gift to the Lord, they bring to the Measurer a pleasant fragrance of words and deeds in that glorious creation, in that bright life.

Praise be to him always, for ever and ever, and the abundance of glory, honour and power, in the heavenly kingdom of the skies. He is by right the king of the world and of the mighty host, wrapped in glory in that beautiful city.
The [Author of light] has granted us that we may here [deserve], and win by good deeds [joys in heaven], where we may seek and possess [the greatest kingdoms] and sit [in high seats],

live in the bliss [of light and peace], possess dwellings [of bountiful joy], enjoy days of glory, see the Lord of victories, [gentle and mild], [without end], and sing praise to him [with everlasting praise], blessed among the angels. [Alleluia].
